newsitem.title: UK: British Treasury adviser sees no need for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: British Treasury adviser sees no need for rate rise.

text.p: There is no immediate need for a rise in British interest rates, but policy will have to be tightened if the pound falls significantly from its current high level, said Martin Weale, an adviser to the Treasury and head of a leading think-tank, on Friday.

In the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) quarterly review, Weale said the recent rise in sterling had knocked almost one percentage point off estimated UK economic growth in 1997.
"In view of the recent exchange rate rise, we now expect GDP growth of 2.5 percent in 1997, almost one percent lower than our last forecast."

It predicted underlying inflation, excluding mortgage interest payments, of 2.1 percent by the end of 1997, adding there was a 60 percent chance of meeting the government's inflation target of 2.5 percent.
"If the exchange rate rise is sustained, we expect the inflation target to be met for the next three years, but growth will be slowed in 1998 and 1999 as well as in 1997," it said.

The pound has soared in value against the currencies of Britain's major trading partners over the last six months, making imports to the UK cheaper and having a dampening effect on inflation, the report said.
But the strong currency also has a depressing effect on the economy as it reduces export demand and encourages imports.
The NIESR predicted export growth would halve in 1997 to 3.5 percent and unemployment would continue to fall to 1.7 million by the end of the year.
"Rapid growth in consumer spending means that growth in manufacturing output is likely to recover despite the high exchange rate," the NIESR's report said.
It said the return of the UK's public finances to a sustainable position was delayed by around one year due to sterling's rise.
"But lower inflation means that there is room for more real spending within the limits of the government's spending targets," the report said.
